questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Honestly, after two years of maintaining a long-distance relationship during a pandemic, it was mostly the chance to be closer to my partner that attracted me. Furthermore, Berlin is a great city with many different things to do and explore and overall just a good place to be.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had hoped that the pandemic was over, but sadly it wasn't. So my stay in Berlin is very much affected by this.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy. The Incoming Erasmus team is great. I both called and emailed them and got the answers and the help I needed, so I would say it was easy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: On the downside, whoever planned the Campus Tour decided we were too many people in my group to go in which meant that I got an outside tour of Campus and was still pretty lost the first time I went inside. All other information events were only, which was also slightly disappointing.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Berlin is a horrible city to find accommodation in. You have to know someone or text at least 50+ people on wg-gesucht. I also subscribed to the WOLOHO newsletter, where I've heard other people have had luck. Best of luck to anyone looking for good (cheap) accommodation in Berlin!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: What surprised me the most was probably how big Berlin actually is. I lived in Neukölln and it took me 30-40 minutes to get to Campus. However, I would still choose to live off-campus or not in student accommodation at any time. The people I knew who lived in such places lived further out from the city, and if you go to Berlin to live the 'big city life', then you should definitely not opt for such a place. They never went into the city to go out because it would take more than an hour to go home in the night, and to me, that's just not worth it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't look into it, so I don't really know how it was.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Everything was online, so it was easy and without any issues.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You get all the information in the emails. Only negative thing is that there are plenty of platforms (Campus Management, Zedat, and a 3rd login place I don't even remember anymore)

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Plenty. I just asked either the professors, the Erasmus coordinators or the Erasmus Office.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got exactly what I wanted. I would've liked to know before that I could've taken courses outside my field of study at Freie, but I figured this out too late. Also, another Erasmus student told me that it's possible to do courses in German and then write the exam in English if you are at a B2ish level of German where you understand most of it, but still lack in writing.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Mainly what I've written above. I don't have any further advice.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Honestly, it wasn't the best. Not compared to UCPH.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I think the level was pretty low. All my courses seemed more like BA-level than MA.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There's still a lot of distance between students and professors at Freie - of course, depending on your course. In some courses, I was only referred to as Miss and then my last name, so it is definitely something else than Denmark and UCPH. One professor was different, though, she was very friendly and less distanced.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Transcreation, Contemporary Britain, Postmodern theories, Narrating the Postmodern, German B2.1 course

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Courses with Ruth Wishart in the English department. It's a lot of fun, and she's a super cool person.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't really encounter any. Berlin is a cheap city to live in if you find good accommodation.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: It's super nice that the transport is in the semester ticket, so when you've paid for your semester, you also have free transport within Berlin and Brandenburg during your semester. Everything else is cheap, my best example being 3,5 euros for a good barista coffee.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They presented some Uni-sports, but I didn't encounter any clubs. However, it was still during a sort of lock-down, so maybe that's why.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I have no idea, honestly.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I don't know.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There is soooo much to see in Berlin. Visit the museums, the parks, the leftover of the Berlin wall, go to Friedrichshagen for a stroll on a Saturday and maybe a dip in the Müggelsee, go to a club for a full night, go see the huge Russian Monument in Treptower Park, go to Potsdam (mostly for the university there, and then you'll wish you went there instead!), get beers in a späti and walk around, to Markthalle 9 for amazing pasta, to the Saturday/Sunday market at Boxhagener or the one at Maybachufer.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Everything is still very much happening in German. I was terrified to go to the Mensa as everything was happening in German and they don't speak any English. Also, the people in front of the libraries, the Zedat center etc. only spoke German (but they were there to check corona-passports, which is fine, but hard when you didn't know you had to book to get in and they couldn't tell you where to book)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Again, I was there during a semi-lockdown, so it was hard to socialize in my opinion.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Possibly the professor-student relationship as it is still super distanced compared to DK.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: In contrast to DK, if you try in (broken) German, they will mostly slow down and let you try out your German instead of just switching to English. I think that's super nice if you actually want to speak German.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Look for accommodation as early as possible, learn some basic German and save money by eating in the Mensa.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not that I can think of, no.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Nothing was rewarding, to be honest. Maybe when I managed to do something fully in German could be considered a small win.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The pandemic. Masks everywhere, booster vaccinations, tests, online class, the uni did nothing to let people (or just Erasmus students) get together.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
